subject: chemistry
title: Elimination from halogenoalkanes
key_idea: A halogenoalkane heated with hydroxide ions can give an alkene by elimination as well as an alcohol by substitution. Hot ethanolic hydroxide favours elimination. In elimination the hydroxide ion acts as a base, not a nucleophile.

blocks.text: Hydroxide ions can react with a halogenoalkane in two ways. This section covers both and the conditions that decide between them.

items.meaning: A reaction in which a small molecule, here HBr or HCl, is removed from a molecule to leave a double bond.
An electron pair donor that attacks a δ+ carbon.

rows: hydroxide ions in water (aqueous NaOH or KOH)
hydroxide ions in ethanol (ethanolic NaOH or KOH)

items: Elimination: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O + Br⁻
The two reactions happen at the same time. The conditions only change which one is the main reaction.

diagram.alt: Pick the conditions for heating 2-bromopropane with hydroxide ions and see which reaction is favoured and what forms.
diagram.prompt: Pick the conditions for 2-bromopropane with sodium hydroxide.

items: Aqueous hydroxide favours substitution. Hot ethanolic hydroxide favours elimination.
Hydroxide is a nucleophile in substitution and a base in elimination.

blocks.text: In elimination the hydroxide ion removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the C–X carbon. This section covers the steps for 2-bromopropane.

items.text: A lone pair on the hydroxide ion forms a bond to a hydrogen atom on a carbon next to the C–Br carbon.
The electrons from the C–H bond move to form a C=C bond between the two carbons.
The C–Br bond breaks. Both of its electrons go to the bromine, which leaves as Br⁻.
Water, bromide ions and an alkene form.

items: Three curly arrows are drawn: from the OH⁻ lone pair to H, from the C–H bond to form C=C, and from the C–Br bond to Br.
Hydroxide ions in ethanol are a stronger base, and the higher temperature favours the alkene.
A hydrogen must be present on the carbon next to the C–X carbon.
Elimination removes H from one carbon and the halogen from the next, forming C=C.
Three curly arrows are needed to show it.

checks.q: State the reagent and conditions that give an alkene from 2-bromopropane.
checks.a: Sodium (or potassium) hydroxide dissolved in ethanol, heated.

checks.q: Explain the role of the hydroxide ion in the formation of propene from 2-bromopropane.
checks.a: It acts as a base. It accepts a proton (removes H⁺) from a carbon next to the C–Br carbon.

checks.q: Give one product of the reaction of 1-bromobutane with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and one product when it reacts with ethanolic sodium hydroxide.

items: Substitution and elimination happen concurrently with the same halogenoalkane and potassium hydroxide, for example 2-bromopropane.
Explain that the reagent hydroxide acts as both a nucleophile (substitution) and a base (elimination).
Outline the mechanism of each reaction with curly arrows.
Know the reaction with ethanolic potassium hydroxide to produce an alkene, where the hydroxide ion acts as a base.
Contrast it with aqueous potassium hydroxide, where hydroxide acts as a nucleophile to produce an alcohol.
Describe the elimination of HBr from bromoethane using NaOH in ethanol and heat to give ethene.
The equation is CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₂=CH₂ + NaBr + H₂O.
